P1.evidence: Strong setter readback used as an opening move rather than a formality: 'I want to hear more about you because I have a brief understanding where you're at right now. I had a chat with Derek. So you've been a wrestler and a power lifter throughout your high school years. That's correct?' The prospect confirmed and expanded immediately. Beyond that, nothing: no four-part frame, no agreement sought, and no open question — the prospect was already self-narrating from the first minute. The cost shows at the end, where the price landed as a genuine surprise: 'I didn't realize it was 6,000.'

P2.evidence: Only two checks were genuinely run. Work was covered well and used later — roofing branch manager, climbing roofs, door-knocking, long driving stints, and the desk-and-car sitting that the rep tied to the mobility protocols. Diet was asked properly: 'Could you walk me through briefly what's your meal plan, like a daily routine?' Everything else is absent. No age, height or weight. No sleep and no energy question. Most seriously, no injury or health-conditions question was asked at all — every clinical fact in this record was volunteered by the prospect into a gap, including a family history of cardiac death, a recurring right knee problem and newly flaring sciatic symptoms. On a call that ends by asking for $6,000 to run six months of ballistic conditioning, not asking the injuries question once is the single largest process failure here.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran in its sharpest form anywhere in this batch and it was a single short question: 'But is it only about the aesthetics or...?' The answer opened everything — 'No, heck no. Man, this is longevity as well. I want my sons to see me be active' — and produced the heart history, the mental-clarity motive and the stress relief. The aesthetics check ran first off the setter note, and the rep tested it honestly rather than accepting it, drawing the useful correction that he is not embarrassed by his body. The who-else question ran directly: 'How do you think how she's going to react to that?' And the legacy thread landed on sons, on his stepson, and on the team he is hiring. The rep also asked the best unscripted question in the batch — 'What's brought you here actually today? You've been, you could do that two months ago, six months ago, a year ago, years ago. Why now?' — which surfaced the marital argument, the family relocation and the gym visit the previous day. That is the material a consequence frame would have been built on, and it was collected and then not used.

P4.evidence: The failed attempt was established vividly, though the prospect volunteered it: $1,000 of home gym equipment bought two years ago, never used, eventually sold, with his wife having predicted exactly that. He named the cause himself — 'it was easy for me to just turn it off and say, I'll do it tomorrow, I'll do it tomorrow' — and named the gap in terms that map straight onto the product: 'once I have my mind made up and it's laid out in front of me and here's a plan' plus 'I also like the accountability.' The rep reinforced with the easy-to-do-easy-not-to-do frame, which functions as P4f. What never ran was the direct questioning: no 'what have you tried', no 'why do you feel it didn't stick'. The equipment story is the best root-cause evidence in the batch and it arrived by luck rather than by asking.

P5.evidence: Never run, for the eleventh consecutive call in this batch. The setup here was as good as it gets: a man with a possible hereditary heart condition, three young sons he wants to stay active for, a two-year record of buying equipment and not using it, and his own words 'I don't want to lose the fire that I have right now'. A single question about what the next two years look like if the fire goes out the way it did last time would have made the August delay very hard to justify. It was never asked.

P6.evidence: The second complete commitment check in this batch, after Patrick Dominguez. The all-in question ran before the price with the identity hook attached — 'if we can figure out all the details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing that work?' — answered 'I am. Yes. Yeah. It's time. There was no hesitation... I wouldn't be on the phone call with you if I had some kind of regret or doubt about it.' The belief question then ran again after the money objection landed, in exactly the right place: 'finances aside, like it does check all the boxes for you?' drawing 'Everything about this is, I'm spot on.' A clear yes was banked before price and re-confirmed after it, which is why the objection that followed was purely financial and never became doubt.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and none of the four steps completed. No payment. No onboarding call with Trevor scheduled. No agreement sent or mentioned. No welcome sequence, no Skool, no onboarding form. The only artefact that reached the prospect was a Payva application link, which he screenshotted and did not submit.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in this batch and the cleanest price hold. The isolation ran first and twice, before any restructuring: 'finances aside, like it does check all the boxes for you?' and 'So the finances would be the only obstacle here?' The most-clients-pay-upfront line ran, with the accountability rationale attached. The monthly surplus question ran verbatim in spirit — 'On a monthly basis, when you cover all the bills, don't know, mortgage, everything, usually what's left in the tank?' — though the answer came back as 'it just varies per month' and was never pinned to a number. The credit score question ran. And critically, asked point blank for a discount — 'tell me what were the lowest that y'all would comfortably accept' — the rep did not name a lower figure and answered with structure instead. That is the correct move and the direct opposite of his handling on the Chris Wiley and Bennu calls. What did not run: the should-versus-how frame, cash on hand, number of cards, available credit total, used versus available, and investments. He also never quoted a monthly figure for the Payva option, so the prospect left without knowing what the affordable version actually costs.

The clearest trigger in the batch and not one move ran. 'At the moment, I won't be able to do that right away, but in about a month, I will be able to', then 'I know for sure I'm going to have to wait until this large check comes through... the third week of August.' The prospect had already supplied the counter-argument himself minutes earlier: 'I don't want to lose the fire that I have right now' and, about the last time he tried, 'I bought $1,000 worth of equipment two years ago to set in my garage, and just sat there.' None of the play was used — no things-never-slow-down, no when-does-it-become-the-right-time, no compounding-cost, no 'what if all you had to do was show up', no only-thing-you-can-control. The rep accepted the August 17 date on first offer and diarised it. A start now on a small first payment against a commission cheque three weeks out was available and never proposed.

Trigger was explicit: 'out of respect for my wife, I'm going to run this by her before I commit to doing either one of those.' One move ran, well — 'When you go to talk to her, how do you feel like how she's going to react?' — and produced a strongly favourable read: she would insist he see it through the way their sons must finish a sport season. The rep then did nothing with that. He never asked whether she would have any reason not to want him healthier, never framed the decision as his own rather than a joint one, and never offered the scripted deposit-and-refund fallback, which is precisely designed for a buyer whose spouse controls the budget and whose money arrives later. Having established there was no likely objection, he closed the topic instead of closing the sale.

SCRIPT GAP — the clinical gate, and the most conspicuous instance of it being ignored rather than merely absent. The prospect volunteered a family history of premature cardiac death: 'there may or may not be some kind of hereditary heart issues in our family. I've had an uncle that passed from a heart attack and his father as well.' The rep's next turn changes the subject to wrestling. Nothing in the playbook requires him to respond, so he did not. He also gave a mechanism for the prospect's recurring knee problem — '95% of the times it's just strengthening that areas' — and dismissed ankle-support footwear as 'total BS'. A clearance question in P2d would have caught all three disclosures at once.

notes: Two things to take from this call in opposite directions. The money handling was the best in the batch: isolated first, financial picture partly run, and a direct request for the lowest acceptable price refused without discounting. Coach that call as the model for OC. The urgency handling was the worst: a prospect who said 'I don't want to lose the fire that I have right now' and who has a documented history of buying equipment and never using it was given a three-week deferral on first offer, with no OD move attempted and no start-now-pay-later option proposed even though a deposit fallback exists in the OB play. Separately, this is the third call in this batch where the rep offers his own declined-hip-replacement story as evidence, and the first where a disclosed family history of cardiac death drew no response at all.
